w:r.w:t: Longitudinal Analysis of Occupancy-Driven Energy Demand in Canadian Residentials
Department of Building, Civil and Environmental Engineering, Concordia University,
The performance gap in building simulations is often driven by static schedules that fail to capture evolving occupant behaviors caused by societal shifts like remote work and demographic aging.
This paper presents a longitudinal analysis of Canadian residential energy demand across five cycles (2005–2025)

. Using General Social Survey (GSS) time-use and Census microdata, we developed a Conditional Variational Autoencoder (C-VAE) framework to generate dynamic, demographics-linked occupancy profiles. These were integrated into neighbourhood-scale simulations for six Neighbourhood Unit typologies in Montreal (Climate Zone 6A). Results demonstrate that weekday occupied hours fluctuated significantly (11.9 to 17.5 hours) rather than following a uniform trend. Compared to conventional defaults, these data-driven schedules consistently increased heating demand by 4–13% and reduced cooling demand by 10–27%. Consequently, we propose residential code calibration factors of +10% for heating and -20% for cooling, alongside periodic recalibration synchronized with national census cycles.

1.2 Challenges and Limitations in Residential Occupancy Modeling

Modeling residential occupancy presents unique challenges compared to the commercial sector, primarily because household life is governed by stochastic individual routines rather than regulated schedules, rendering standardized deterministic assumptions such as ASHRAE baselines ineffective and directly contributing to the building energy performance gap
. Even within similar demographics, energy profiles diverge substantially due to intra-household social dynamics that models simulating occupants in isolation systematically overlook
. Compounding this are logistical and ethical barriers to high-resolution data: intrusive sensing raises privacy concerns
, PIR detectors often lack granularity to distinguish individuals
, and Time-Use Surveys fail to capture long-term behavioral consistency or seasonal variation
. Methodological trade-offs further persist between Agent-Based Models and Markov chain approaches, balancing behavioral detail against computational tractability and temporal dependency capture

, while the lack of BPS standardization forces co-simulation workflows that remain beyond typical practitioner capacity. Finally, models developed for specific climatic or cultural contexts generalize poorly across built environments
1.3 Existing Approaches in Occupancy Modeling and Their Deficiencies
The representation of occupant behavior in building performance simulation has evolved from static to dynamic approaches, yet significant limitations persist across all four modeling typologies
. Deterministic models relying on ASHRAE or ISO schedules remain the industry norm but fail to capture behavioral stochasticity, producing energy discrepancies of up to 41%

. Stochastic models such as Markov Chains partially address this through probabilistic transitions, yet their memoryless property and inability to capture intra-household social interactions limit residential accuracy
. Data-driven and agent-based approaches offer higher resolution but introduce prohibitive computational costs, black-box interpretability issues, and privacy concerns
. Across all methodologies, the neglect of household social dynamics, poor long-term temporal consistency, and the persistent scalability-accuracy trade-off remain unresolved

TUS serve as a foundational empirical source for occupancy modeling, capturing the contextual "who, what, when, and where" of daily life and enabling researchers to link activities to demographic characteristics

. Stochastic methodologies such as Markov Chains transform this raw diary data into continuous simulation inputs, while clustering techniques generate representative urban archetypes for bottom-up energy modeling of metabolic heat gains and appliance-driven peak demand

. However, TUS data faces inherent limitations: single-day snapshots fail to capture seasonal variation or long-term habit consistency, self-reporting biases introduce memory and time-rounding artifacts, and the absence of spatial resolution necessitates secondary inference to map activities to specific thermal zones

This study develops a data-driven framework for generating longitudinally consistent occupancy datasets capturing the demographic composition and temporal behavioral patterns of Canadian residential occupants across a twenty-year period (2005 to 2025). This study utilizes two complementary national datasets managed by Statistics Canada to construct comprehensive occupancy profiles for residential building energy modeling: the Census of Population and the General Social Statistics Program (GSSP) Time Use cycle. Conceptually, the Census provides the rigid demographic structure of Canadian households
covering household size, dwelling type, occupant age distribution, gender composition, and family structure
while the GSSP animates this structure with behavioral and temporal dynamics through 24-hour retrospective time diaries recorded at 10-minute intervals
. Census data from four cycles (2006, 2011, 2016, and 2021) were

employed, noting that the 2011 cycle utilized the voluntary National Household Survey with reduced response rates (68.6% versus 93.5% in 2006), while mandatory status was reinstated in 2016, restoring reliability with response rates exceeding 98% by 2021

. The GSSP Time Use cycles of 2005, 2010, 2015, and 2022 capture evolving lifestyle patterns over two decades, with the 2022 cycle incorporating enhanced measurement of telework and remote work patterns in response to post-pandemic societal transformations. By linking Census-derived household characteristics with GSSP-derived temporal patterns, this integrated approach generates comprehensive occupancy datasets that address the critical limitation of conventional building energy models, which typically rely on generic, static occupancy assumptions that fail to represent the diversity and temporal evolution of actual Canadian households.

Ensuring longitudinal consistency across four Census cycles (2006, 2011, 2016, 2021) required a systematic harmonization pipeline standardizing disparate microdata file structures through four sequential stages: raw file parsing and cleaning, variable name harmonization and categorical unification

of GSSP Time Use data presented substantially greater complexity due to evolving activity classification systems: the 2005 and 2010 cycles used ACTCODE with 182 and 264 unique codes respectively, while 2015 and 2022 transitioned to TUI_01 with 64 and 121 codes. To establish longitudinal consistency, a master activity classification framework comprising 14 standardized categories was developed through systematic codebook analysis (

To address the limitation that each GSS record represents an individual respondent rather than a household, a conditional generation methodology synthesized internally consistent multi-occupant diaries by constraining subsequent household members' schedules through co-presence compatibility rules, producing synchronized household occupancy profiles suitable for BEM integration.

A critical challenge in integrating the two datasets was the absence of explicit dwelling type information in GSS records. To address this, a machine learning classification approach was implemented to probabilistically assign Census-derived dwelling types to GSS household records using shared demographic linking variables — household size, occupant age distribution, household composition, and geographic region. Analysis of Census dwelling type distributions across the four study periods revealed significant temporal shifts in Canadian housing stock composition, as illustrated in

3 Classification of GSS Dataset Using Historic GSS Cycles

The integration of Census and GSS datasets for dwelling type classification required addressing a fundamental structural incompatibility: Census data exist as single household-level records, while GSS data are bifurcated into person-level demographic files (Main File) and episode-level time-use files (Episode File). The Main File contains static attributes
one row per respondent with variables such as age, sex, household size, and income
while the Episode File contains multiple rows per respondent representing sequential activity episodes.

To enable classification, these structures were consolidated through a many-to-one left join using the unique respondent identifier (PUMFID) as the linking key, broadcasting static demographic attributes onto all associated episode records (

). Given the substantial scale of GSS Episode Files (millions of records), a memory-efficient chunked processing architecture was implemented, reading files incrementally in blocks of 100,000 rows with sequential merging to prevent computational overflow. Following consolidation, variable name standardization was applied through a harmonization dictionary mapping GSS-specific nomenclature to Census conventions (e.g., PRV→PR, HSDSIZEC→HHSIZE), ensuring consistent feature naming for subsequent machine learning classification tasks.
3.2 Generative Temporal Framework for 2025 Occupancy Classification

A fundamental limitation of census-based occupancy modeling is the absence of nationally representative data for future projection years. While Census and GSS datasets provide empirical foundations for historical periods (2006, 2011, 2016, 2021), building energy simulations for contemporary decision-making require occupancy profiles for years beyond the most recent census cycle—specifically, 2025 in this study. Traditional supervised classification approaches (e.g., Random Forest, Gradient Boosting) prove inadequate for this temporal extrapolation task because they assume static demographic-dwelling relationships; training a single model on pooled multi-year data forces the algorithm to learn an "average" association that is incorrect for any specific time period, as the relationship between household demographics and dwelling types evolves substantially across decades due to urbanization, housing market dynamics, and socio-economic shifts. Furthermore, census data are cross-sectional rather than longitudinal—different households are sampled in each cycle
precluding the use of sequential modeling techniques (e.g., Recurrent Neural Networks) that require tracking individual entities through time.

To address this challenge, a generative temporal framework was developed that models not individual household classification, but the evolution of population-level demographic distributions conditioned on dwelling characteristics. The methodology employs a Conditional Variational Autoencoder (C-VAE) to learn low-dimensional "archetype" representations of household demographics in the latent space, conditioned on stable building features (dwelling type, construction period, tenure status)
. This unsupervised representation learning captures the statistical essence of demographic profiles associated with specific dwelling types across all historical periods.

emporal drift modeling tracks how these demographic archetypes shift over time by fitting autoregressive models to the evolution of mean latent vectors across census cycles (2006→2011→2016→2021), enabling extrapolation to 2025.

, the trained decoder generates synthetic 2025 household demographic profiles by sampling from the projected latent distribution conditioned on user-specified building stock compositions, producing statistically consistent occupancy datasets for periods lacking empirical census data. This approach transforms the problem from static classification to dynamic population synthesis, leveraging the temporal structure inherent in sequential census cycles to forecast plausible demographic futures.
3.3 Multi-Phase Generative Pipeline: Architecture and Workflow

The generation of 2025 occupancy datasets required a six-phase pipeline integrating representation learning, temporal forecasting, household assembly, behavioral matching, dwelling type refinement, and energy model conversion, as illustrated in

. The foundation of the pipeline is a multi-head Conditional Variational Autoencoder (C-VAE) trained on harmonized historical census data, compressing demographic attributes (age, income, household size) and building conditions (dwelling type, tenure) into a 128-dimensional latent space through an encoder-decoder architecture with
and sigmoid output heads for mixed data types.
. From historical census data to 2025 building energy model-ready occupancy schedules
The model was trained for 100 epochs using the Adam optimizer

, converging to a total loss of 3.89 after 100 epochs. Reconstruction performance was reported separately by variable type. For categorical variables (dwelling type, marital status, employment class, and similar), the decoder recovered the original category in more than 80% of records, indicating that the latent representation retains the discrete structure of the input rather than collapsing minority categories into the majority class. For continuous variables (age, household size, income), the decoder reproduced more than 92% of the variance of the original values, indicating that the latent representation also preserves the magnitude and

dispersion of the input rather than reverting to the cycle-wise mean. The combination of these two indicators confirms that the 128-dimensional latent space carries enough information to regenerate Canadian household demographics with both categorical fidelity and quantitative accuracy
, confirming that the latent space captures sufficient complexity to represent Canadian household demographics.

To project this learned representation forward to 2025, a Cluster-Based Vector Momentum (CBVM) framework was employed rather than population-level average drift, which would erase demographic diversity through regression-to-mean effects. K-means clustering (K=8) identified persistent demographic archetypes across census cycles (2006–2021) — such as young urban renters, established suburban families, and retired homeowners — and characteristic velocity vectors were computed by tracking centroid trajectories across sequential periods, with a decay factor of 0.95 per five-year interval preventing unrealistic divergence.

Model reliability was assessed through a hindcasting protocol in which the C-VAE and the CBVM drift component were trained exclusively on the 2006, 2011, and 2016 cycles, then used to project the 2021 population without exposure to any 2021 data. The projected distribution was compared against the held-out 2021 Census across age, household size, dwelling type, and income variables. The hindcast preserved the multimodal shape of the household-size distribution, the right-skew of the income distribution, and the age-pyramid asymmetry between renting and owning households — structural features that a population-mean drift model would regress toward the cross-cycle centre. This reproduction of distributional shape (Appendix A1) provides the principal evidence that the same machinery, advanced one further cycle, can be expected to project the 2025 population without collapsing to a temporally averaged mean

Following latent space projection, synthetic 2025 agents were assembled into structurally coherent household units through a priority-based matching algorithm enforcing demographic consistency constraints
appropriate spousal age differences, parent-child age relationships, and household size targets
transforming 15,000+ disconnected synthetic persons into realistic family units.

Each synthetic agent was then linked to an empirical time-use schedule from the harmonised GSS library through a cascading four-tier matching strategy. Tier 1 attempted an exact match across all ten demographic variables (age group, sex, household size, marital status, employment class, work hours, occupation, province, and transportation mode). Tier 2 relaxed the criterion to the five energy-driving variables (household size, work hours, age, sex, employment class), recognising that these dominate occupancy and metabolic heat. Tier 3 retained only the structural constraints (household size and age group), and Tier 4 served as a failsafe matching on household size alone. The 2025 synthetic cohort comprises 323 generated households, intentionally smaller than the empirical cycles. The 323-household figure was sized to populate every cell of the downstream stratification grid (household size × dwelling type × age class × employment status) used in the BEM Monte Carlo, while remaining tractable for the parallel EnergyPlus pipeline. Distributional convergence with a hypothetical full-cycle draw was assessed through hindcast validation against the 2021 Census rather than by enlarging the synthetic cohort itself.

3.5 BEM Setup, Occupancy Integration, and Simulation Framework

Energy simulations were conducted for Montreal (Climate Zone 6A) using four DOE/ASHRAE 90.1 Prototype Building archetypes: single-family detached houses (2-storey, 110 m²), attached row houses (2-storey, 180 m²), mid-rise apartments (4-storey, 784 m²), and high-rise apartments (10-storey, 784 m²). Each archetype was configured with thermal and construction characteristics typical of post-1980 North American housing stock, with building envelope and HVAC characteristics held constant across all occupancy scenarios to isolate the impact of occupancy schedule variation from physical building changes. . Application of the Presence Filter Algorithm to Household Load Profiles
To quantify the impact of empirically derived occupancy patterns on residential energy demand, a comparative simulation framework evaluated six scenarios per Neighbourhood Unit: Default (standardized

Apartment schedules), 2025 (C-VAE synthetic projection), and four empirical GSS cycles (2005, 2010, 2015, and 2022), yielding 36 scenario-neighbourhood simulation pairings across Montreal. Household selection followed a three-stage filtering protocol retaining only single-detached households with 2 to 4 persons, matched to a target working-day occupancy profile through Sum of Squared Error minimization, with the 100 best-matching households selected per scenario-neighbourhood combination. This controlled ensemble isolates behavioral evolution effects from occupancy category differences, though it necessarily excludes non-standard work patterns such as shift and remote workers — identified as a priority for future investigation. End-use disaggregation reported lighting, equipment, fans, heating, cooling, and domestic hot water intensities separately across the 100-household Monte Carlo ensemble per pairing, with results aggregated to the neighbourhood scale and presented as mean and standard deviation in Section 4.

4.1.4 Household Size Influence on Occupancy Patterns
Population-average occupancy schedules obscure substantial heterogeneity arising from household composition differences.

disaggregates 2025 GSS-derived presence patterns by household size, revealing a counterintuitive inverse relationship between household size and occupancy probability. Weekday occupied hours decline systematically from 18.2h (1-person) to 5.2h (5-person), a 71% reduction, with daytime occupancy fractions dropping from 56.1% to 12.4%. This reflects the probabilistic nature of household-level measurement: single-person dwellings register as occupied whenever the sole occupant is present, whereas multi-person households register as occupied only when at least one member remains home, with midday probabilities suppressed as multiple members simultaneously depart for work and school. Weekend patterns follow similar inverse trends but with elevated overall presence (19.2h to 6.9h; 63.8% to 21.7% daytime fractions), reflecting reduced employment and school obligations.
. Presence schedules by household size (1–5 persons): hourly profiles (a,b) and metrics (c,d)

This 71% variation in weekday occupied hours is one of the most policy-consequential findings of this study. Population-average schedules simultaneously overestimate presence in large households, inflating internal gains and cooling loads, and underestimate occupancy in single-person dwellings, suppressing predicted heating loads precisely when sole occupants maintain near-continuous presence. For multi-family residential buildings with diverse unit compositions, a single Default schedule applied uniformly across a building stack will oversize cooling for family units while

heating for single-occupant units. Segment-specific modeling accounting for household size distribution would improve load prediction accuracy, support more targeted HVAC control strategies, and provide a more defensible basis for dwelling-type-differentiated corrections in residential energy codes.

Section 4.2 propagates the occupancy patterns characterised in 4.1 through neighbourhood-scale building simulations to quantify their energy consequences: annual end-use impact across all six Neighbourhood Units (4.2.1), temporal trends in scenario deviation from Default (4.2.2), diurnal and seasonal demand profiles (4.2.3), peak load timing and magnitude (4.2.4), and whole-neighbourhood energy fingerprints (4.2.5). Simulations were conducted for Montreal (Climate Zone 6A) using TMYx weather files, comparing Default archetype schedules against Monte Carlo ensembles of empirically-derived GSS household profiles across the five temporal cycles.

presents the deviation of each GSS-derived temporal scenario from the Default baseline across four end-uses (Heating, Cooling, Electric Equipment, and Domestic Hot Water), disaggregated by neighbourhood unit. GSS-derived schedules consistently increased heating demand by +3.9% to +12.6% and reduced cooling demand by -10.3% to -27.1% across all neighbourhood units,
confirming a consistent occupancy-driven signal across all six Neighbourhood Units.

The 2025 synthetic projection produced the most moderate deviations (+5.4% heating, -11.9% cooling), while the 2005 and 2015 empirical cycles generated the largest divergences, consistent with their 60% daytime occupancy fractions.

w:r.w:t: . Peak Cooling and Equipment Load Timing by Occupancy Scenario

GSS-derived profiles simultaneously shift appliance-driven Equipment peak loads toward evening hours (17:00 to 18:00), consistent with the return-home activity concentration documented in Section 4.1.1. This temporal decoupling between the Equipment peak and the Cooling peak carries a consequential asymmetry: evening equipment loads accumulate when ambient temperatures are already declining, partially offsetting the equipment-cooling interaction

that sustains Default's afternoon peak. The pattern is directionally consistent across all six neighbourhood units, confirming that occupancy schedule choice alters peak timing regardless of dwelling density or archetype composition. For grid operators, the

advance in peak cooling toward 13:00 and the concurrent evening shift in equipment loads mean that demand-response dispatch strategies currently calibrated to mid-afternoon residential peaks would mistime curtailment signals under contemporary occupancy patterns, suggesting that utility-side flexibility programs should reassess their dispatch windows in line with census-cycle occupancy updates.
4.2.5 Internal Gain Coupling and Neighbourhood Energy Fingerprint

presents the neighbourhood energy profiles as normalized radar charts, with five end-use spokes (Heating, Cooling, Electric Equipment, Domestic Hot Water, and Lighting) normalized to Default = 1.0 and one polygon per GSS temporal scenario across all six NUs. We term this end-use signature the neighbourhood energy fingerprint, analogous to a spectral signature, because its shape uniquely identifies the coupling between occupancy regime and dwelling typology. The Default spoke values reflect the full range of neighbourhood typologies, from heating-dominated detached clusters (RC
: 156.5 kWh/m²/yr Heating, 45.4 kWh/m²/yr Cooling) to apartment-dominated mid-rise and high-rise units (
: 35.2 kWh/m²/yr Heating, 18.1 kWh/m²/yr Cooling), confirming that the absolute energy profile differs substantially by typology even before occupancy schedule variation is applied.

Across all neighbourhood units, the occupancy-driven transformation produces a consistent shape change rather than a uniform rescaling: Heating spokes extend beyond the Default circle while Cooling spokes contract inside it simultaneously, with Equipment and DHW spokes shifting modestly. The 2005 and 2015 empirical cycles produce the most pronounced fingerprint distortion across all six panels, consistent with their 60% daytime occupancy fractions generating the largest internal gain deviations. The 2025 synthetic projection produces a more compact polygon that

approaches the Default circle in all NUs, visually confirming the convergence trend identified in Section 4.2.2 while preserving the directional heating-cooling asymmetry that persists even under moderated behavioral assumptions.

Default schedules systematically misrepresent Canadian residential occupancy by overestimating mean occupancy by 32% (68.4% vs. 46.5%) and metabolic heat generation by 24% (95W vs. 72.1W), translating directly into heating underestimation of 3.9 to 12.6% and cooling overestimation of 10.3 to 27.1% across all six Montreal NUs (Figure 15). The neighbourhood energy fingerprints (Figure 21) confirm this correction is a genuine end-use shape transformation rather than a uniform rescaling, with heating and cooling spokes shifting in opposite directions while Equipment and DHW remain comparatively stable.

The occupancy–energy coupling persists consistently across the full density gradient from suburban detached clusters to urban high-rise nodes. Because the integration pipeline is identical for every archetype and operates at the same per-building resolution whether executed on a single IDF or on a batched neighbourhood ensemble, this consistency reflects a thermophysical mechanism rather than an artefact of scale-specific schedule handling. The contribution of the neighbourhood-scale framing is therefore one of
, exposing the same coupling across six dwelling configurations representative of the Canadian residential stock, rather than a methodological departure from building-scale work.

The non-monotonic trajectory across cycles reflects competing forces: the unexpectedly lower 2022 occupancy relative to 2015, despite post-pandemic remote work adoption, is tentatively attributable to enhanced telework activity reclassification in the 2022 GSS cycle, demographic cohort transitions, and the rising apartment share documented in Section 2, though disentangling these mechanisms requires longitudinal panel data beyond the scope of cross-sectional GSS cycles.

The practical implications span design, operations, and policy. The 18% cooling oversizing estimate derives from the 17.4% peak cooling intensity reduction in Section 4.2.4 (Figure 20) combined with the schedule-driven daytime load reductions confirmed across all scenarios in Figure 15. Canadian residential codes should consider correction factors of approximately +10% for heating and -20% for cooling relative to Default assumptions, with periodic recalibration synchronized to census cycles to prevent compounding errors over decadal code lifespans. The

advance in peak cooling toward 13:00 further suggests that demand-response dispatch strategies calibrated to mid-afternoon peaks would mistime curtailment signals under contemporary occupancy patterns. The 71% variation in weekday occupied hours across household sizes (Section 4.1.4) additionally argues for dwelling-type-differentiated schedule corrections rather than a single national Default. Limitations include the restriction to Montreal and post-1980 archetypes, exclusion of shift and remote workers, the smaller 323-household 2025 synthetic sample, reliance on pre-2022 demographic trajectories, and a dwelling-type classifier calibrated on pre-2016 Census data. Future work should extend the framework to additional climate zones, incorporate household-size-segmented simulations, and couple evolving occupancy patterns with housing stock turnover models to project grid-level impacts at the national scale.

This research established a replicable framework integrating Canadian Census and General Social Survey data through a Conditional Variational Autoencoder pipeline to produce longitudinally consistent occupancy schedules spanning 2005 to 2025, directly addressing the performance gap introduced by static Default assumptions in residential building energy modeling.

empirically-derived occupancy schedules increase predicted heating demand by 4 to 13% and reduce predicted cooling demand by 10 to 27% across six Montreal Neighbourhood Units relative to Default assumptions. These deviations stem from Default's 32% overestimation of mean residential occupancy (0.684 vs. 0.465) and 24% overestimation of metabolic heat generation (95 W vs. 72.1 W).

To our knowledge, the C-VAE and Cluster-Based Vector Momentum framework presented here is the first to produce longitudinally consistent Canadian occupancy schedules spanning two decades of empirical GSS cycles and extending to a synthetic 2025 projection, offering a nationally representative and replicable methodology for constructing period-specific occupancy inputs suitable for direct integration into building energy models.

The policy implication is clear: residential building codes calibrated on static schedules accumulate compounding errors over decadal lifespans and should be recalibrated in synchrony with census cycles to remain representative of the populations they govern. As Canadian residential behaviour continues to evolve in the wake of remote-work adoption and demographic aging, building performance modeling must treat occupancy as a dynamic, empirically-grounded boundary condition rather than a fixed design assumption, or the performance gap will persist, and widen, over time.
